RFC Compliance Report

How far Ze meets each RFC it implements, and the tests that prove it. Source: internal/le/rfc, rfc/short/*.md, and rfc/audit/*/*.json.

How to read this page

This page shows how far Ze meets the standards (RFCs) it implements, and how that is proven. For each RFC, Ze keeps a summary of the requirements identified so far and links them to their tests. Automatic checks read those summaries and tests, and the figures on this page are computed from the same summaries and tests.

If you are evaluating Ze for one role, start with Coverage by profile. To check one RFC, find it in the RFCs included in automatic checks table and open its own page, which lists each requirement and the tests behind it. The glossary below explains the results and notes the corresponding terms in Ze's source.

Glossary of the terms this page uses
Summary
Ze's file for one RFC: it lists the RFC's requirements, the tests behind each one, and the support status Ze publishes for the RFC.
Requirement
one obligation an RFC states, kept in the summary with an identifier such as RFC4271-8.2.2-12 that names the RFC and its section.
MUST-level (mandatory)
a requirement stated with MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT. The optional levels are MAY, NOT RECOMMENDED, OPTIONAL, RECOMMENDED, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT.
Included in automatic checks
an RFC whose mandatory requirements are checked against its summary and tests. Other RFC summaries are listed at the end of the page with the reason they are excluded. The repository calls this enrollment.
Automatic compliance check
the check reads RFC requirement summaries and tests to find missing evidence or unsupported claims. The repository calls it a gate.
Positive and negative test (polarity)
a positive test proves Ze does what the requirement demands; a negative test proves Ze refuses what the requirement forbids. Tested both ways means both exist.
Test linked to a requirement
one test that names the requirement it checks in a source annotation. One requirement can have several tests.
Recorded fault test
evidence that a test can detect a fault: the code under the test was broken once on purpose, the test was seen to fail, and a record stores what the test, its claim and the code looked like. The break is not run again. Ze's source calls this a discrimination record.
No fault test recorded
a test record states that no deliberate code change could demonstrate the test failing. The source calls this escaped, and it does not count as proof that the test can detect a fault.
Outdated fault test
a test, its stated claim, or the code it checks has changed since the fault test was recorded. The source calls this lapsed, and it no longer counts as proof.
Gap
a requirement the summary openly declares Ze does not meet yet. Every gap is work Ze owes.
Annotation
a note on a requirement, written in braces, that says why it needs no ordinary pair of tests. {single-polarity}: the requirement admits no counter-case, so one direction plus a recorded reason is the whole proof. {not-applicable}: the obligation does not bind Ze. {feature-declined}: the obligation applies only to a feature the RFC makes optional and Ze does not offer. {lower-layer}: a layer under Ze performs the behavior, on state Ze installs into that layer. {gap}: a declared gap. A partial requirement has tests for part of it; the rest is unmet or unproven and earns no credit.
Linux cannot do this
a verified kernel limitation prevents the required primitive. The annotation names the Linux Limitations Register entry. The row is OS blocked: a limit of the kernel, never counted against Ze, so it sits with the rows not owed and in no section of the MUST bar.
Requirements reviewed
a reviewer read the original RFC sentence by sentence and checked the requirement list against it. The review record documents that check. Requirements not reviewed means that this check has not been completed, so the RFC is excluded from the coverage figures.
Excluded sentence
a sentence of the RFC that the review decided not to turn into a requirement, with a kind and a reason.
Test review
a reviewer's recorded judgment of whether the tests check what the requirement says. Fresh means still current. Shifted means the test is unchanged and only the surrounding file moved. Stale means the reviewed code or requirement changed.
Ze proven, Ze MUST proven (bar segment)
a MUST row Ze's own code performs, with a tagged test whose recorded break was seen to fail.
OS verified (bar segment)
a row a layer under Ze performs (the Linux kernel Ze ships, or a Go library Ze links), with a tagged test that checks that layer's behavior on the state Ze installs, and a recorded break.
Proof pending (bar segment)
a row with a tagged test and no recorded break proving it yet, that neither the summary nor a test review says Ze does not meet.
OS testing gap (bar segment)
a row a layer under Ze performs, with no verified test of that behavior yet. It is a gap in testing, not in correctness.
Exclusion unchecked (bar segment)
a row claimed not to bind Ze whose evidence is still to be checked. Until it is, the row stays among the rows Ze owes.
Not assessed (bar segment)
a row no tagged test covers and that neither the summary nor a test review says Ze does not meet, so nothing yet says whether Ze meets it.
Not built (bar segment)
a row the summary or a test review says Ze does not meet, including a row built only in part.
SHOULD proven (bar segment)
a SHOULD or MAY row Ze's code performs, with a tagged test whose recorded break was seen to fail.
Not owed (bar segment)
a row that does not bind Ze, shown by checked evidence: it binds a role Ze does not fill, it applies only to an optional feature Ze does not offer, or Linux cannot provide its primitive (OS blocked). It is left out of the MUST bar.

For RFCs whose requirement lists have been reviewed, the bars and Total row group those requirements by status: proven by Ze's tests, verified in the operating system, not applicable, or awaiting implementation or tests. Coverage by profile

A profile groups the RFCs one kind of deployment needs. If you are evaluating Ze for one role, its profile page gives the figures for that role alone.

This page covers every RFC. Each deployment role and technology has its own page showing mandatory and overall coverage, with the RFCs it builds on listed first: RFC coverage by profile.

Who implements each document

Some RFCs are carried out by Ze's own code, some by a layer under or beside Ze, and some oblige no implementation at all. This section says which is which, because the figures on this page count only what Ze's own code is held to.

The ledger counts what Ze implements in its own code. An RFC implemented by another layer is excluded from these checks and names what performs it, and where Ze can observe the behavior the requirement still carries a test over the state Ze installs.

Not every sentence of an RFC becomes a requirement. This section counts the sentences a review left out, by the reason given, so you can check what was left out and why.

A reviewer reads the original RFC sentence by sentence and decides which sentences become requirements. A sentence left out is recorded with a category and a reason, and is absent from the requirement list. This differs from the Out of scope card above, which counts requirements that exist and carry a {not-applicable} annotation. Check results

Compliance is checked in several groups. Each line below says what one group verifies and whether it passed, and for a group that failed, what that means for the figures. The raw findings, written for Ze's contributors, are in the collapsed block after the list.

No open issue. Every mandatory requirement included in the checks has positive and negative tests, or a note explaining why not.

  • Requirement lists: Passed. Each RFC's requirement list is readable and consistent: requirement identifiers are not reused or lost, each requirement quotes the RFC text it cites, and the links it declares between RFCs and profiles agree with the RFC texts.
  • Test evidence: Passed. Every gated MUST-level requirement has its tests, or an annotation that says why not, test evidence already recorded is not lost, and every test that claims a requirement compiles and is named for what it covers.
  • Requirement annotations: Passed. Every annotation that excuses a requirement from Ze's own tests still names code that exists, quotes the RFC sentence it relies on, or names a verified blocking kernel entry in the Linux limitations register with evidence for that exact requirement at the shipped kernel version.
  • Published ledger rows: Passed. Every enrolled RFC with an unmet requirement renders a public row that discloses it, a public row never disappears while its summary remains, and each summary's enrolment disposition gives a reason a reviewer can check.
  • Reviewer verdicts: Passed. Each reviewer verdict recorded on a requirement is well formed and still describes the code and tests it judged.
  • Recorded breaks: Passed. Each recorded break still matches the test, the claim and the code it was recorded against, and no recorded proof is lost.
  • Reviews of RFC text: Passed. Each sign-off of a sentence-by-sentence review of an RFC's text is valid and current.

The MUST bar shows mandatory requirements (MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL and SHALL NOT) that Ze and its operating system must meet. It includes only RFCs whose requirement lists have been checked against the original text. Ze proven means a test has been shown to fail when the required behavior is deliberately broken. Behavior provided by the operating system or a library is OS verified when a test checks it using the settings Ze installs and has also been shown to detect a deliberate fault; until then, it is an OS testing gap. Proof pending counts requirements a tagged test covers that no deliberate fault has yet been shown to break and that nothing records as unmet. Exclusion unchecked counts requirements claimed not to apply to Ze whose evidence is still to be checked. Not assessed counts requirements no tagged test covers and that nothing records as unmet, so nothing yet says whether Ze meets them. Not built counts requirements the RFC summary or a test review says Ze does not meet, in full or in part. The overview bar adds optional requirements (MAY, NOT RECOMMENDED, OPTIONAL, RECOMMENDED, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT) and requirements that do not apply to Ze. An RFC marked requirements not reviewed is excluded from these figures because its requirement list has not been checked against the original text. Counts are loaded from the RFC data files.
